name: Torres del Paine National Park
blurb: Guanaco, puma and condor between the Paine massif and the Patagonian steppe.

tip.title: Remove the guanaco
tip.text: Guanaco are the main prey of the puma here. Set Guanaco to -100% and watch the puma, then the condor and culpeo that share its prey.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Torres del Paine National Park

notes: The species list comes from GBIF occurrence records inside a circle around the park, so it can include nearby areas. Feeding links come from GloBI records and the sources listed where they state them; others are general ecology and are illustrative.

nodes.desc: Short, cool summers with long daylight drive growth of grasses and shrubs; the forest line is set by cold and wind.
Meltwater from the Southern Patagonian Ice Field feeds the rivers and lakes of the Paine massif and the moist valleys below it.
Thin soils of steppe, shrubland and forest hold the nutrients that plants draw up and that decomposers return.

nodes.name: Soil microbes and fungi
nodes.desc: Break down dead plants, dung and carcasses, returning nutrients to the soil.
Dominant tree of the Magellanic subpolar forest, tolerant of deep cold and regrowing readily after fire. Its leaves are food for South Andean deer elsewhere in Patagonia.
A Patagonian shrub whose berries are eaten by thrushes and other birds, which GloBI records.
A common small rodent of Patagonian steppe and forest; one of the many small mammals eaten by pumas, foxes and raptors.
Introduced to the Southern Cone for hunting. It grazes grasses and herbs and is now a major prey of culpeo, pumas and raptors.
Grazing goose of steppe and wetlands, feeding on leaves, stems and seeds. Foxes take many of them.
Common bird of shrubland and forest edges that eats berries such as prickly heath, and spreads their seeds.
Endangered deer of Andean forest and scrub. It browses plants such as lenga; the cougar is its only natural predator.
The main large grazer, eating grasses, shrubs and herbs. Park numbers rose from about 175 in 1975 to about 3,000 by 1993.
Opportunistic fox that eats hares and rodents, and sometimes young guanacos and birds.
An opportunistic raptor and scavenger; GloBI records it eating hares and carrion of livestock.
Mainly a scavenger on large carcasses, found by sight; it also raids nests for eggs and rarely takes small live prey.
Top predator of the park. It preys on guanaco and huemul, and its kills feed scavengers such as condors.
